requirements.text:
clamp(x, lo, hi) reads its arguments as signed integers. It returns lo when x < lo, else hi
when x > hi, else x.
requirements.reason: This claim states the required signed comparisons and returns lo, hi, or x in the specified order for every 32-bit input combination.

requirements.text:
gcd(a, b) reads its arguments as unsigned integers and returns their greatest common divisor,
with gcd(a, 0) = a.
requirements.reason: This claim interprets both inputs as unsigned 32-bit values and returns their greatest common divisor for every pair, including gcd(a, 0) = a.

requirements.text: sum_to(n) reads n as an unsigned integer and returns 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1), wrapped to 32 bits.
requirements.reason: This claim sums the unsigned values from 0 through n−1 for every 32-bit input and converts the result to 32 bits, giving the required wraparound behavior.

claims.summary: The exported sum function always returns the sum of all nonnegative integers below its input, reduced to 32 bits.
claims.name: Examples.Toy.sumTo
claims.intent: `sum_to(n)` on unsigned 32-bit ints: `0 + 1 + … + (n − 1)`, wrapped to 32 bits.
details: Covers every 32-bit input, interpreted as an unsigned natural number from zero through the maximum 32-bit value.
Returns the sum of the integers from zero up to, but not including, that unsigned value, reduced modulo 2 to the 32nd power.
Returns also guarantees the module can be instantiated and every call terminates without trapping under every host behavior.
caveats: The sum is computed as a natural-number sum and then reduced to 32 bits; it is not a signed sum.
The claim does not specify the internal algorithm, runtime, or memory effects beyond the stated return behavior.

claims.summary: The exported clamp function always returns one of its inputs, selected by signed comparisons against the supplied bounds.
claims.statement:
∀ (x lo hi : BitVec 32),
  FVA.Wasm.Exec.Returns Examples.Toy.Lifted.module "clamp"
    [FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 x, FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 lo, FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 hi]
    [FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 (if x.slt lo = true then lo else if hi.slt x = true then hi else x)]
claims.name: Examples.Toy.clamp
claims.intent:
`clamp(x, lo, hi)` on signed 32-bit ints: `lo` if `x < lo`, else `hi` if `x > hi`, else `x`
(tested in this order, so with `lo > hi` the result is `lo` for `x < lo` and `hi` otherwise).
details: Covers every combination of three 32-bit inputs: a value, a lower bound, and an upper bound.
Compares all three as signed 32-bit integers; it returns the lower bound if the value is below it, otherwise the upper bound if the value exceeds it, otherwise the value.
There is no arithmetic here that can wrap around; the selected result is one of the inputs.
Returns also guarantees instantiation and termination without a trap for every host behavior.
Example input lists (negative values denote signed inputs): [0, -1, 1], [-2, -1, 1], [2, -1, 1], [0, 1, -1], [-2147483648, 0, 2147483647].
caveats: If the lower bound is greater than the upper bound, the nested comparisons still select a value by the stated order; the claim does not assert conventional clamp behavior for that case.
The specification gives no separate guarantee about memory effects or the implementation's algorithm.

claims.summary: The exported gcd function always returns the greatest common divisor of its two inputs, treated as unsigned 32-bit values.
claims.statement:
∀ (a b : BitVec 32),
  FVA.Wasm.Exec.Returns Examples.Toy.Lifted.module "gcd" [FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 a, FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 b]
    [FVA.Wasm.Exec.Val.i32 (BitVec.ofNat 32 (a.toNat.gcd b.toNat))]
claims.name: Examples.Toy.gcd
claims.intent: `gcd(a, b)` on unsigned 32-bit ints: their greatest common divisor (`gcd(a, 0) = a`).
details: Covers every pair of 32-bit inputs, each interpreted as an unsigned natural number.
Returns their greatest common divisor, reduced modulo 2 to the 32nd power; the greatest common divisor itself is no larger than either input.
Returns also guarantees instantiation and termination without a trap for every host behavior.
caveats: The inputs are treated as unsigned numbers, even if a reader might regard a 32-bit value as signed.
The claim specifies the mathematical greatest common divisor of the unsigned input values, reduced to 32 bits; it does not guarantee a particular algorithm.
